difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY because it tests one concept (FD implication via attribute closure), where a single closure computation, (VW)+ = {V, W, X, Y, Z}, settles three options and the fourth is the union rule, taking a prepared student about a minute.
stem:
Given the relational schema $R = (U, V, W, X, Y, Z)$ and the set of functional dependencies:

$$
\{U \rightarrow V,\ U \rightarrow W,\ WX \rightarrow Y,\ WX \rightarrow Z,\ V \rightarrow X\}
$$

Which of the following functional dependencies can be derived from the above set?

solution.quick: Use attribute closure. $(VW)^+$: $V \rightarrow X$ adds $X$, then $WX \rightarrow Y$ and $WX \rightarrow Z$ add $Y, Z$, so $(VW)^+ = \{V, W, X, Y, Z\}$. It contains $Y$ and $YZ$ but not $U$. $WX \rightarrow YZ$ is the union of two given FDs. Derivable: **(A), (B), (D)**.

steps.title: The test for a derivable FD
steps.body:
Let $F = \{U \rightarrow V,\ U \rightarrow W,\ WX \rightarrow Y,\ WX \rightarrow Z,\ V \rightarrow X\}$. An FD $\alpha \rightarrow \beta$ can be derived from $F$ (using Armstrong's axioms: reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity) **if and only if** $\beta \subseteq \alpha^+$, where $\alpha^+$ is the attribute closure of $\alpha$ under $F$.

To compute $\alpha^+$: start with $\alpha$, and repeatedly add the right side of any FD whose left side is already contained in the set, until nothing changes.

steps.title: Compute (VW)⁺ (needed for A, C, D)
steps.body:
| Step | FD applied | Why it fires | Closure so far |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | – | start | $\{V, W\}$ |
| 1 | $V \rightarrow X$ | $V$ is in the set | $\{V, W, X\}$ |
| 2 | $WX \rightarrow Y$ | $W, X$ are in the set | $\{V, W, X, Y\}$ |
| 3 | $WX \rightarrow Z$ | $W, X$ are in the set | $\{V, W, X, Y, Z\}$ |

$U \rightarrow V$ and $U \rightarrow W$ never fire, because $U$ is not in the set. So

$$
(VW)^+ = \{V, W, X, Y, Z\}, \qquad U \notin (VW)^+.
$$

steps.title: Compute (WX)⁺ (needed for B)
steps.body:
Start with $\{W, X\}$. $WX \rightarrow Y$ adds $Y$ and $WX \rightarrow Z$ adds $Z$; $V \rightarrow X$, $U \rightarrow V$ and $U \rightarrow W$ cannot fire. So

$$
(WX)^+ = \{W, X, Y, Z\} \supseteq \{Y, Z\}.
$$

Equivalently, $WX \rightarrow YZ$ is just the **union rule** applied to $WX \rightarrow Y$ and $WX \rightarrow Z$.

steps.title: Check each option
steps.body:
| Option | FD | Relevant closure | Right side contained? | Derivable? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (A) | $VW \rightarrow YZ$ | $\{V, W, X, Y, Z\}$ | $\{Y, Z\}$: yes | Yes |
| (B) | $WX \rightarrow YZ$ | $\{W, X, Y, Z\}$ | $\{Y, Z\}$: yes | Yes |
| (C) | $VW \rightarrow U$ | $\{V, W, X, Y, Z\}$ | $\{U\}$: no | **No** |
| (D) | $VW \rightarrow Y$ | $\{V, W, X, Y, Z\}$ | $\{Y\}$: yes | Yes |

An explicit Armstrong derivation of (A): from $V \rightarrow X$, augmentation by $W$ gives $VW \rightarrow WX$; union of the given FDs gives $WX \rightarrow YZ$; transitivity gives $VW \rightarrow YZ$. Decomposition of (A) then gives (D) $VW \rightarrow Y$.

(C) fails, and a two-row instance proves it: take $t_1 = (u_1, v, w, x, y, z)$ and $t_2 = (u_2, v, w, x, y, z)$ with $u_1 \ne u_2$. Every FD in $F$ holds (the two rows differ on $U$, so $U \rightarrow V$ and $U \rightarrow W$ hold vacuously, and they agree on everything else), yet the rows agree on $VW$ and differ on $U$, so $VW \rightarrow U$ is violated.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: The derivable FDs are $VW \rightarrow YZ$, $WX \rightarrow YZ$ and $VW \rightarrow Y$, i.e. options **(A), (B), (D)**.

solution.teaching:
**Functional dependencies and their consequences.** An FD $\alpha \rightarrow \beta$ on a relation says: any two tuples that agree on the attributes $\alpha$ must also agree on $\beta$. Given a set $F$ of FDs, other FDs follow automatically. The set of all of them is the closure $F^+$. Armstrong's axioms generate $F^+$ and are sound and complete:

1. **Reflexivity:** if $\beta \subseteq \alpha$ then $\alpha \rightarrow \beta$.
2. **Augmentation:** if $\alpha \rightarrow \beta$ then $\alpha\gamma \rightarrow \beta\gamma$.
3. **Transitivity:** if $\alpha \rightarrow \beta$ and $\beta \rightarrow \gamma$ then $\alpha \rightarrow \gamma$.

Useful derived rules are **union** ($\alpha \rightarrow \beta$ and $\alpha \rightarrow \gamma$ give $\alpha \rightarrow \beta\gamma$), **decomposition** ($\alpha \rightarrow \beta\gamma$ gives $\alpha \rightarrow \beta$) and **pseudo-transitivity** ($\alpha \rightarrow \beta$ and $\gamma\beta \rightarrow \delta$ give $\alpha\gamma \rightarrow \delta$).

Searching for an axiom chain by hand is slow and error-prone. The practical test is the **attribute closure** $\alpha^+$: the set of all attributes that $\alpha$ determines. Compute it by starting from $\alpha$ and firing every FD whose left side is already inside, until no FD adds anything. Then $\alpha \rightarrow \beta$ is derivable exactly when $\beta \subseteq \alpha^+$. The same closure also finds keys: $\alpha$ is a superkey when $\alpha^+$ contains every attribute.

FDs are **one-directional**. $U \rightarrow V$ says $U$ determines $V$, not that $V$ determines $U$. An attribute that appears on no right-hand side, like $U$ here, can only ever be determined by a left side that already contains it.

**Back to this question.** $(VW)^+$: $V \rightarrow X$ brings in $X$, and then $W$ and $X$ together fire $WX \rightarrow Y$ and $WX \rightarrow Z$. So $(VW)^+ = \{V, W, X, Y, Z\}$, which contains $Y$ and $Z$ but not $U$. Hence (A) and (D) are derivable and (C) is not. (B) is the union of two given FDs. (Here $U^+ = \{U, V, W, X, Y, Z\}$, so $U$ is the only candidate key.)

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: $(VW)^+ = \{V, W, X, Y, Z\} \supseteq \{Y, Z\}$. Chain: $V \rightarrow X$ augmented by $W$ gives $VW \rightarrow WX$, and $WX \rightarrow YZ$ (union) then gives $VW \rightarrow YZ$ by transitivity.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $WX \rightarrow Y$ and $WX \rightarrow Z$ are both given, so the union rule gives $WX \rightarrow YZ$ directly; equivalently $(WX)^+ = \{W, X, Y, Z\} \supseteq \{Y, Z\}$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: $U \notin (VW)^+ = \{V, W, X, Y, Z\}$. $U$ appears on the right side of no FD, so it cannot be derived from attributes that exclude it. The two rows $(u_1, v, w, x, y, z)$ and $(u_2, v, w, x, y, z)$ satisfy every given FD but violate $VW \rightarrow U$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: $Y \in (VW)^+$. It also follows from (A) by decomposition: $VW \rightarrow YZ$ implies $VW \rightarrow Y$.

solution.shortcut: $U$ is on no right-hand side, so nothing without $U$ on its left can determine $U$: reject (C) at once. (B) is the union rule. One closure, $(VW)^+ = \{V, W, X, Y, Z\}$, confirms both (A) and (D).
solution.commonTrap: Reversing FDs: from $U \rightarrow V$ and $U \rightarrow W$ it is tempting to conclude $VW \rightarrow U$, but FDs only go one way, so (C) is not derivable. The opposite slip is to reject (A) and (D) because $X$ is not in $VW$, overlooking that $V \rightarrow X$ supplies $X$ so that $WX \rightarrow Y$ and $WX \rightarrow Z$ can fire.

answerVerification.notes: An attribute-closure computation gives (VW)+ = {V, W, X, Y, Z} and (WX)+ = {W, X, Y, Z}, so VW -> YZ, WX -> YZ and VW -> Y are derivable and VW -> U is not. The check also confirms a two-tuple counterexample (rows equal except on U) that satisfies every given FD but violates VW -> U. This gives A;B;D, matching the official key A;B;D.
